newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Debt issuance in Q4 surpasses all records - BIS.
newsitem.headline: Debt issuance in Q4 surpasses all records - BIS.

text.p: Global financial activity remained in high gear during the fourth quarter of 1996 with issuance of new debt surpassing all previous records, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said on Thursday.

Searching for high returns, investors explored new financial instruments, but also showed increasing willingness to take greater risks, BIS said in its quarterly report on international banking and financial markets.
The international securities market was at the core of this buoyant market and the issue of new international bonds and euronotes rose to a record $163.6 billion in the fourth quarter.
For the full 1996 year, the issue of new securities rose 18 percent from 1995 for total outstanding debt of $3.2 trillion. In 1995 securities issuance rose 13 percent, BIS said.
Activity in the syndicated loan market was also heavy in the fourth quarter with new announcements of $155.7 billion for an increase of 69 percent for the full year to $523.7 billion.
Financial institutions remained particularly active and accounted for two-thirds of new debt as they raised capital on an unprecedented scale through increasingly complex instruments.

However, Basle-based BIS, central bank to the world's central banks, said this growing securities issuance by financial institutions may have represented a shift in the structure of risk management rather than a genuine increase in financing of real economic activity.

Against a backdrop of limited scope for a further substantial reduction in interest rates in major markets, investors' search for higher returns led to a broadening of activity to include new currencies, such as the Argentine peso and the Croatian kuna.

With ample global liquidity, the reduction in risk premiums boosted demand for securities that involved the repackaging of assets or derivative features. Most new issues in the fourth quarter incorporated one of both elements, BIS said.
With such complex features, BIS questioned whether investors really understood the risks they were taking and whether bond issuers were getting their money too cheaply.
"However, questions remain as to whether the risk and return characteristics of complex structures, as well as the liquidity of underlying assets, have been properly assessed by investors," BIS said.
Detailed data from the third quarter showed brisk lending to developing countries, but this masked a sharp cutback in credit to Asian countries, BIS said.
Lending to developing countries from major industrial nations accelerated to $34.7 billion in the third quarter from $28.1 billion in the second quarter.

There was a pronounced fall in lending to Korea and Thailand, partially as a result of efforts by national authorities to reduce reliance on short-term debt, but also a reassessment of lenders strategies.
Another feature of banking activity was the continued retreat of Japanese banks from other major financial centres.
In the syndicated loan market, the proportion of acquisition-related transactions in the fourth quarter rose to 23 percent from 18 during a year where corporate merger activity rose to new records.
Borrowers from the U.S. accounted for the bulk of new credits with favourable terms granted to industrial borrowers encouraging several to return to the market after long absence.
Financing activity by emerging countries also proceeded at a strong pace in the fourth quarter with Korean borrowers benefiting from the country's entry into the OECD.
But while borrowing margins for developing countries moved upward slightly, there was also a slight rise in the spreads charged to industrial country borrowers.

"Nevertheless, concerns were expressed by some regulators. U.S. bank supervisors in particular, made renewed calls for caution in the dollar loan market, noting that the pricing of some transactions did not appropriately reflect risks," BIS said.
